title: Added a "What is it?" mode to my AI-built browser game: every control gets a lettered ring you can click to learn what it does
author: Harlan_42
selftext:
I'm building **To Battle**, a single-player digital version of Milton Bradley's 1962 **Broadside** naval board game. I'm writing the code with Claude Code, and the art is AI-generated.

The screen has a lot of controls: map type, coast number, seeds, saves, play-as, old rules, full screen and more. Early players kept asking what half of them did, so I added **What is it?**

**How it works**

* Click **What is it?** and every control on screen gets a lettered ring, A through Z
* Click a ring to open a card that names the control and explains what it does
* **Next ▶** steps through the rings in order, so it doubles as a guided tour of the screen
* **Help** goes back to How to Play, and clicking **What is it?** again turns the rings off so play carries on

**How it came together**

* I asked the AI to go through the screen, identify every feature and write a brief overview of each one. It got about 90% of them on the first pass. The board features were the gap, so I detailed those out myself
* It landed on exactly 26 features. Good thing there weren't more, because we're out of letters
* It started as a help submenu, but once every control had an overview, it made more sense as a full feature that covers the whole screen
* The happy accident was the **Next** button. Players can tour every feature by clicking in the same place, with no hunting around the screen for the next ring

I like it better than a tutorial because it's on demand, it never blocks the game, and it explains the screen the player is actually looking at.

**Try it:** [https://battle.harlan42.com](https://battle.harlan42.com) (desktop or tablet)

How are you handling onboarding in your AI-built games? Guided tours, tooltips, or letting players figure it out?
